utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What's happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've asked to make an application before the witness continues, and I ask to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to make an application regarding the Defence's special defence involving the accused's mental capacity. Rule 67 requires notification of such defence as early as practicable and, in any event, prior to the commencement of trial. When I saw that the accused, according to the case history --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw that the accused, according to the case history, had been treated in a psychiatric facility around the period of the crime, I became concerned and, approximately one year ago, asked whether there would be a psychiatric defence and was told that there would not. The first time any type of notice was given of this defence was in the Defence Pre-Trial Conference, after the Prosecution had rested. However, that notice was vague and did little to provide the information the Prosecution needs in order to conduct a proper inquiry into the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What page was this said?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the Pre-Trial Conference, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it the Pre-Trial Conference? You said after the Prosecution had rested, I thought you must have meant the Pre-Defence conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. I stand corrected, Your Honour, the Pre-Defence Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you give us the page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can't at this point, Your Honour. I will after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was said?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic -- I mean, Mr. Domazet stated that there would be evidence of the psychiatric condition of the accused. I had objected at that time and raised the requirements of Rule 67. The Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My recollection was we referred specifically to whether there was a defence of diminished responsibility being raised, so-called defence perhaps I should describe it, because it goes only to sentencing, and I was told there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's why I'd like to have a look at what was said. This seems to proceed upon the assumption that my understanding was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess, Your Honour, what's concerning me at this stage is that we've already heard the accused say that at the time the crimes were committed, he had spoken with the devil and with God. We've heard from Dr. Vasiljevic say that, on the 2nd of June, it was his assessment that he was suffering from psychoses. My concern is, to me it wasn't clear that this is not a defence. In fact, I'm under the impression that all of these witnesses here are being called to testify regarding his mental condition at the time of the commission of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But we still haven't been given notice, and if we haven't been given notice, then the Defence has to establish why they should be entitled to rely upon such a defence. But my concern at the moment is it may not be a defence of diminished responsibility. In my experience of these cases to date in this Tribunal has been that some sort of inchoate, indescribable mental state is asked to be taken into account in order to explain that the accused may have done something which he ordinarily would not have done. That goes to sentencing still; it does not go to any question of criminal responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, my main concern is, and perhaps Mr. Domazet can clear up this fact at this point, is whether this defence is being raised as a special defence to negate the mens rea of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't negate the mens rea of the crime. Insanity would. But that's not even suggested. We are waiting, are we not, for a report from the psychiatrist who examined the accused over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, and that is part of my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that's where we should go. Let's find out what's in the report instead of trying to conjure up all sorts of issues from the way in which this evidence is being led, let's find out what the psychiatrist says, and if there's a problem about it, then there will be a lot of trouble if it does amount to something which has been denied throughout by Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the difficulty that the Prosecution is having is that I'm being called upon to cross-examine these witnesses without the benefit of this report yet. I would ask, can Mr. Domazet give us some kind of preliminary assessment? He certainly must have talked to this expert since the weekend. Can we have some idea of what the findings of this expert are so that I may be able to cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I asked him to do on Friday. But none of these witnesses so far have suggested that any such psychoses had any effect upon his understanding of what he was doing or his intention to do whatever he did. Not one of them has; and they're all doctors, they could have said so. And the fact that they haven't will certainly tend against any case that is put up to the contrary later. He's had two doctors there, and each of them could have given an opinion and they weren't asked. Now, that's a fairly good start to a rejection of anything that may come up later. But nevertheless, you are certainly entitled. I thought this is something that could have been done between counsel. Why it has to be done by us, I don't know. Have you asked Mr. Domazet what is the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I've asked him to let me know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Have you asked him since the weekend?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I talked to him yesterday about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Now, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He said that he will be speaking with the expert last evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Let's just simply ask, "What are the issues?" and then we'll find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And there's just one other matter, Your Honour. As a precautionary matter, I requested from Uzice hospital through the RS government any medical records and received a reply that there were no additional records aside from the ones that were seized pursuant to an order of the Chamber. Yesterday and on two different occasions, it became -- or documents were produced here in Court and eventually tendered into evidence comprising those records from Uzice. I would ask that I be provided immediately with all documents that the Defence is going to rely on, either for alibi or for this special defence if it is being raised, and that I be provided with translations. I was provided with four documents yesterday afternoon, and I had translators work overtime last night, but it certainly makes it difficult for the Prosecution to adequately prepare its case when it's provided these untranslated documents hours before it's expected to cross-examine witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Domazet, I have already remarked upon the fact that you've been in this case for well over a year and all of these issues had become apparent during that time and it is, if I may say so, very unhelpful to be met with documents at this stage which have never been translated and which should have been given, pursuant to the Rules, at least a year ago. First of all, have you got any more medical records?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said yesterday, the books that we brought today are the last we have, and only four pages out of those books are, in our opinion, relevant for the Vasiljevic case, which I yesterday gave to Mr. Groome photocopies of, and those are probably the four pages that he mentioned were being translated. That is all we have as documentary evidence. However, I would like to add something in connection with this evidence from Uzice. The request mentioned by Mr. Groome through the government of Republika Srpska is something I know nothing of, but the Government of Republika Srpska is not competent for Uzice as Uzice is in Serbia, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So the request could only have gone through the Yugoslav government and not Republika Srpska. As far as Uzice is concerned, I must inform you of a major problem that we had when, on November the 1st last year, when these documents were seized from Dr. Moljevic when he brought the originals to Visegrad and since he thought that all that would be needed was him to show those documents and to give photocopies. After that, we really were not able to obtain anything from Uzice, and the situation has changed only recently, and we managed to have these witnesses personally bring these documents. So I really am sorry that this occurred in this way, but I have nothing else than what I gave Mr. Groome yesterday and which we intend to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can certainly understand the reluctance of the Serbian hospital at Uzice to produce any more documents after the seizure, but that's a risk which the Prosecution ran in seeking the order which they obtained. And certainly Republika Srpska, apart from its general unhelpfulness, would not have been likely to be able to get anything from Uzice. My concern at this stage, though, is you have said twice those are the only documents you have. Do you expect any others to come or have you requested any others to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, unless the Prosecution raises the issue of making further requests from the Uzice hospital. Then I would make an effort to obtain them. But as far as we are concerned, we have no other documents, nor have we made any requests for additional documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, that's that one out of the way. Now, what has happened in relation to your psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke to Mrs. Lopicic yesterday, who interviewed and examined the accused on Saturday and Sunday. She carried out the various interviews and tests, everything that was necessary. She has compiled documents, and I asked her to prepare a written report as soon as possible, to have to translated into English. I hope that that will be in a day or two, and certainly before the end of the week. She left for Belgrade this morning, and she promised that she would be working on the report today and tomorrow and send it to us. As soon as I receive it, I will provide copies for Mr. Groome and Your Honours immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But has she indicated to you what the general nature of her conclusions are? I think we're entitled to ask this. You've waited 12 months to have this done, and we are now getting towards the end of the trial, so I really do think we are entitled to find out from you what your understanding is of what issue is going to be raised, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it really is very difficult for me to say when she didn't tell me what her final finding would be. She didn't wish to do so before she examined all those documents, so that I really am unable to say what her conclusion will be. I know that she told me that the disease described here as psychosis was not only due to alcoholism, that it is a mental disease. To what extent that will affect her conclusion, that is, that at the critical time he had diminished responsibility or significantly diminished responsibility which would affect the sentence should the guilt of Mr. Vasiljevic be proven, or his total irresponsibility, I'm afraid that I am unable to say until I get that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be that we will have to, in effect, hive off the sentencing proceedings because we cannot allow this to keep on as a running issue of which the resolution is not yet in sight. It is something which really has caused immense problems. It may mean that in such sentencing proceedings, if it comes to that, that these doctors who saw him at the time will have to be recalled. But the Prosecution can't be put in the place, by your failure to do the organisation of this 12 months ago, that they are embarrassed because they have not had the opportunity of exploring these issues with the very doctors who saw him at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour, should that be the conclusion of the report, but all I can do is promise that I will do my very best to have that report in the next few days and certainly before the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just to correct, I misspoke earlier. The request to Uzice hospital was made through the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the transcript reference would be 1820 for the Pre-Defence Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure what on 1820 is relevant. We're talking about the problems that Mr. Domazet had about continuing for four weeks unbroken. Page 1821 is where you raise it. Yes. Well, at that stage, it was clearly pointed out that if there was anything in this report that was to be obtained from the psychiatrist relating to the so-called special defence, you would be entitled to have the accused and any other witnesses recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm simply requesting at this time, since we have a line-up of psychiatric doctors and nurses who treated him, if I could have some indication -- I mean, I think we've heard Mr. Domazet's response, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet's response is rather like that of a character in a famous television series of “I Know Nothing, I come from Barcelona," I think was the expression. He simply says he doesn't know. Well, this is very unfortunate and, as I've pointed out on a number of occasions, this is something that should have been investigated 12 months ago. But we can't prevent the accused running that issue, but I want to emphasize throughout that it is something which, at this stage, could go only to the issue of sentencing, and if necessary, bearing in mind the time constraints that we have, if when this report comes and it does go only to the issue of sentencing and if you do need to ask the accused further questions, and the doctors, then we'll hive off that as a separate proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That seems to me, from a practical point of view, the only way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But if it comes up with something worse than that, if it comes up to some form of insanity, which would go to the issue of criminal responsibility, then we'll just have to grind to a halt. I don't know when we're going to finish the case, but it's going to have to be fitted in, with some difficulty, during the course of six cases running at once during the course of next year. At the moment, we have a window of two weeks at the beginning of the year to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Was that the only matters that you wanted to raise? Can we go on with the witness? Yes. Bring Dr. Simic in, please. Mr. Groome, there's something in the opening address at pages 1836 to 1837 which, unfortunately but perhaps understandably, leaves it completely open about a reference to a mental state and accountability at the critical time. So you can put that down as a reference that you should go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have kept you waiting. We had to resolve yet another problem that keeps arising in this case. Mr. Domazet, you were examining the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We shall continue the discussion we had yesterday afternoon. If you remember, I was asking you questions about your recollections about Mitar Vasiljevic as your patient at your ward in July 1992. Could you tell me what you remember about this patient.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have said the most important things that I do remember. One must bear in mind that ten years has gone by and that virtually all patients at the psychiatric ward have a very similar clinical symptoms. What separated him out from the rest and what makes me remember him better is that he was transferred from a different ward of our own hospital, which is not so frequently the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please look at the case history document and the diagnosis entered in the case history so that you can comment, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P136.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that the case history?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is an abstract from some document from a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I apologise. P138. I do apologise. Have you had a look at it, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, has this refreshed your memory in any way? Could you tell us a little more about the diagnosis entered in the case history?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This diagnosis is psychosis 298.9. This is on the basis of the Ninth International Classification of Disease, which has now been changed. 298.9 are so-called undefined or unclassified psychoses. This diagnosis was established most frequently when there was no specific psychopathological substratum which could be separately classified, so that this diagnosis indicates that there was a serious mental disorder which, in this case, was manifested by disturbed behaviour, agitation, disquiet, a disturbance of his thought process, and that is what was dominant in this case. In the case history, one can see the amnesia when the patient's wife was consulted and it was established that he consumed a lot of alcohol and that he was treated three times at the ward because of alcoholism. In addition to that, mention is made of the death of a close relative. These are all factors which could have contributed to this grave mental disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, according to you, this diagnosis is an indication of a grave mental disorder. My question is: Is this linked to alcoholism, if we are dealing with an alcoholic, or may that be the case or not necessarily so? So could you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite certain that this was a case of alcohol-provoked psychosis, we would need to have information of his previous treatment, and this has not been attached to this case history for us to be able to see how the disease of alcohol abuse developed in the patient and what degree of damage it provoked, leading to this disorder. We would also need to have the follow-up of this case history, that is, his subsequent treatment, to see how his disease developed further; whether he had any fresh disorders, whether he was treated later on or admitted to medical institutions for similar conditions. So that in this specific case, there is a high degree of probability that this psychosis could have alcohol in its etiology, that is, that alcohol abuse may have provoked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as his condition then is concerned, that is at the time he was brought to your ward, could you tell us, on the basis of what you know now, anything about his ability to comprehend acts and consequences of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. those acts when he was admitted to your ward in the condition in which you described.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be clearly seen here, regarding his psychological state, that is, his mental condition, that he was extremely agitated, that his thought process was upset, that he cannot concentrate, that he is able to answer only a question here and there, that it is difficult to establish contact with him; that he was singing, shouting, resisting control, and that other functions could not be assessed. And as a result, the patient was tied up, which is something we described and went into yesterday, how this is done and why, which is an indication that, at that point in time, he was not able to control his behaviour or to be conscious of his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now take a look at the same exhibit, on page -- I think it's page 3, and it refers to the patient's discharge. You have the page in front you. Would you please read through it and tell me what it says, what it's about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The patient is calm but still a little accelerated. The date is the 28th of July 1992. At the request of his wife, he is being discharged, sent home for further treatment in outpatient -- as an outpatient. And the signature is Vasiljevic Milojka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, does this mean that, at that point in time, he had been relatively cured or not, or was he just being released because of the request made by his spouse?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like to say he was partially cured; not cured, partially cured. So he -- it was necessary for him to remain in hospital a little while longer. However, by law, the next of kin - that is to say, parents, guardians, or spouses - have the right to take the patient out of hospital, out of the ward, at their own personal request and at their own responsibility, at their own risk, and that was this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that his condition had improved compared to what it had been previously, or had it not been the case, would you have been able to prevent his next of kin taking him out of hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here that the patient is calm and orderly, which speaks of his conduct, his behaviour. And at that time, that means that his conduct was satisfactory. Mention is only made of the fact that he is accelerated and the term used in our terminology means that effective behaviour is a little raised in the sense of greater psycho-motor functions. However, I assume that this state was also satisfactory in terms of his wife, so that she decided to take him out of hospital because very rarely does somebody take a patient out who is not feeling well or is showing marked signs of still being sick. So this was a patient who was visibly -- whose condition was visibly improved, and they did not have the patience for waiting for end of treatment to be completely cured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the first page of the exhibit, please, and tell me, first of all, how the case history was filled out and how it goes -- is moved from ward to ward. Do -- are entries made on each ward? In this particular case history, regardless of what was written in the previous ward, for example, orthopaedics in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we can see that the case history was opened at the orthopaedics department. They opened the case history form, printed form. They began writing in entries. And in the case history, we see that it says that the patient was transferred to the psychiatric ward. After the psychiatric ward, he was moved to a third ward -- had he been moved from the psychiatric department to a third ward, they would have continued writing in entries in this same case history form.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In concrete terms, Dr. Simic, would you take a look at the columns and tell us whether column 12 was filled in in your ward, and also column 11. Were columns 11 and 12 filled in in your ward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Column 12, where it says "Psychosis," that was filled in at our ward. And I think I typed this out myself. It looks like the typewriter I used at the time. And also, there's my signature at the bottom. Using that same typewriter, it is printed out and typed out using the same letters. And I also filled in the date of discharge. Probably there should be a discharge list which I wrote too, but I can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I have here a discharge list which is from your particular ward. Now, I'm going to show it to you to see whether that is the discharge list and whether it refers to this particular patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to show the original and the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there an English version of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I don't believe, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had a draft drawn up last night. I'll have copies made. But it's simply a draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Really, Mr. Domazet, this is not well done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is the document the photocopy of which I gave to Mr. Groome yesterday. I omitted to mention that. And there are really no more exhibits, pieces of evidence that have not been handed over. So I omitted to say that I gave him this photocopy yesterday, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's probably only stating the obvious, Mr. Domazet, but you have not produced an English version, which you are required to do. And you may have produced it to Mr. Groome in order for him to have it translated, but you haven't given us any translation. We shouldn't have to rely upon Mr. Groome to give them to us. Anyway, you proceed, and we'll have to rely upon the interpreters when you read matters to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have you had a look, Doctor, at this discharge list?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it the discharge list that you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you read what it says on the discharge list, the diagnosis, and the description underneath, so that we can have it interpreted.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discharge diagnosis of the patient, Mitar Vasiljevic, psychosis 298.9. In the epicrisis, it states that the first hospitalisation, the first hospitalisation existed, then he was transferred to orthopaedics. Upon admission he was exceptionally restless, agitated; he was singing, shouting, resisting -- offering resistance upon arrival; his train of thought was disturbed by incoherent speech. After receiving treatment, his condition improved so, at the request of his wife, he is being released home to be given further treatment as an outpatient. Laboratory findings within normal limits. Suggestion for treatment: Largactil tablets, 100 milligrams, three times a day one tablet, a control check-up with the relevant psychiatrist in 14 days. Until then, to be relieved of duty. Control check-up with the orthopaedist. It is signed by the unit doctor, Dr. Slobodan Simic, and the head doctor of the ward or unit, Dr. Borislav Martinovic, neuropsychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, just one moment, please. Doctor, can you help us with this word "epicrisis"? According to my medical dictionary, its meaning depends upon its pronunciation, which is never a good start, but I think this is the relevant one and I'd like you to confirm it. It means a critical summary or analysis of the record of a case. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A summary would be closest to the meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, with respect to treatment and medicaments, can you tell us what kind of drugs were suggested and was that sufficient, in your view at that time, the drugs that were suggested?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The patient was given what we call -- the generic term is Chlorpromasin, which is an anti-psychotic, in fact. Its dominant effect is a sedative. The optimum dosage is 300 milligrams per day. At that time, it was the drug that we prescribed to patients suffering from the kind of clinical picture that Mr. Vasiljevic had, where there was a predominance of agitation and restlessness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, you see for yourself from the case history what the patient was like, and you said that he was transferred from the orthopaedics ward. Do you happen to remember, from what he said or from what others said, how Mitar Vasiljevic had been injured? How was he injured?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we heard the story about the patient who had fallen off a horse and was, as a result, brought to the orthopaedics ward and was very restless and agitated there, and because of his behaviour, he was transferred to the psychiatric ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just one more point. Would you take a look at page 1 of Exhibit 138, the case history. Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Take a look at the top, and underneath the words "Case history," what has been typed out immediately underneath that heading. It says: "Injury on the battlefield in Visegrad." That's what it case in the case history. Can you explain what the term "Ratiste" or "battlefield," "battleground," "front," what it meant.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not a highly professional question. For all of us, the battleground or battlefront was any territory where fighting took place for -- and especially for us in Serbia, at that time, the battlefield was Bosnia, because this patient was brought to us from Bosnia and we were Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that when it says "battlefield," that that, for you working in your hospital, meant people who were in the theatre of war, and in this concrete case, that was Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, was this what you wrote for all patients coming in with injuries from that territory or did it apply to those who were actually injured during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I was not an administrative worker in charge of the administration. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And the terminology that you used when you saw the word "Ratiste" or "battlefield," it meant what you have just explained to us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My name is Dermot Groome and I will be asking you questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Regarding the question of when Mr. Vasiljevic first entered Uzice hospital, you yourself have no personal knowledge about when that occurred; is that correct? You just know when he arrived at the psychiatric facility.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in 1992, you said that you were, I believe, a general practitioner on the psychiatric ward. Can you tell me, at that point in time, were you treating the patients for their psychiatric illnesses or were you simply treating them for other ailments and other doctors were treating them for their psychiatric maladies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was what we call a secondary doctor, that is to say, a doctor preparing to specialise in the field of psychiatry, but he has not been accorded the -- a psychiatric specialist training yet. So I did treat psychiatric patients along with direct -- in direct cooperation with my mentor, the psychiatrist. So I was waiting to get a place for the psychiatric specialisation. Let me also say that there were very few of us so that I was the only secondary doctor or young doctor on the ward, and the ward had 50 beds and, at the time, only four specialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would I be correct in saying that you were treating these patients for their psychiatric ailments but it was under the supervision of your mentor? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would they have to approve any medication that you sought to prescribe or any other therapies that you sought to prescribe to a patient?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who would you say had the most direct contact with Mr. Vasiljevic -- I'm sorry. Which doctor would you say had the most direct contact with Mr. Vasiljevic during his time on the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the most direct contact and, through me, my mentor, Dr. Slavica Jevtovic, the lady doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that all aspects of Mr. Vasiljevic's treatment, you would have been the primary person who was made aware of whatever was occurring with Mr. Vasiljevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about this classification of 298.9. You told us that that was an old classification, meaning unclassified psychoses, from the Ninth International Classification of Disease. What I'd ask you is can you tell us, if you were classifying these symptoms today, what would be the classification that you would use?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today's classification, the Tenth International Classification of Disease, the code would be F23, acute transient psychotic disorders. That would most probably be the diagnosis for this patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've used the word "transient." Does that mean that this is a passing psychosis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: F23 in the classification is explained as acute and transient, depending on the type, the case. But at all events, an acute psychosis, acute psychotic disorders are transient, but in a certain number of cases, they represent a manifestation of a more serious psychological disorder, and in certain cases, a reaction to certain conditions or factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there any subcategories of this F23 which would more aptly describe the condition of Mr. Vasiljevic or is it one general category?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are subcategories. However, essentially it is a general diagnosis. The subcategories, if you're interested in hearing them -- do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Only those subcategories that you may feel more accurately describe the condition of Mr. Vasiljevic at the time you treated him.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would probably have been diagnosed as F23.1. Sorry, .0.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could you give us the name of that subcategory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all the same category but subcategories of acute transient psychotic disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've just told us that in certain cases, this transient psychosis is a reaction to certain conditions or factors. Can I take from that that this can be brought on by a particular precipitating event that happens in the life of a person? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it possible that somebody who had suffered the loss of somebody close to them could be affected in this way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could it also be true that a person who perhaps did something terrible, the guilt and the realisation of what they had done caused them to react in this way? For example, let's say a man killing his wife. Could that be the type of event that could bring on this type of psychosis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are categories of stressful events which may trigger it, but such a case is not mentioned as being one in that category. It probably hasn't been encountered in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if somebody were to lapse into psychosis because of the realisation of something that they had done, are you saying that you would classify that differently than the F23.1 or .0?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the patient gave a psychotic picture, then he would be classified as a F23.0 and the other subcategories, but we would have to see the etiological factor that led to the manifestation of this psychotic disorder. It is far more frequent in practice - as I used to work in a prison hospital with psychiatric patients who had committed a crime - in an enormous number of cases, the patient first develops this psychotic disorder and only then commits the felony or the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your experience, have you come across cases where the person has committed the crime and subsequently develops a mental disorder?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not had occasion to come across a patient in the prison hospital who first committed the crime and then developed psychosis. All the patients had either -- either developed this psychosis and then committed the act or committed the act without suffering from the psychosis but having some other mental disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In Serbia, are there provisions for committing patients who a doctor may feel are a threat to himself or to other people? In other words, be sufficiently insane that a doctor can apply to have the person committed for treatment? Is there a provision under Serbian law?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can address that issue at two different levels. If the patient falls ill from a psychotic disorder and if this is manifested in his case by aggressive and out of the ordinary behaviour, he is hospitalised, put in a hospital, and treatment is undertaken. After treatment, he is discharged home. However, in cases when the patient suffering from psychosis commits a criminal offence - manslaughter or attempted manslaughter or is a threat to the environment - the so-called security measure is prescribed, which means treatment and commission to a closed-type institution. And this ruling is made by the court upon the proposal of the doctor or upon the request of the family and the damaged party.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, under Serbian law, you would have been entitled, if you thought that Mr. Vasiljevic's mental disorder were serious enough, you would have been entitled to invoke this procedure through your mentor to have him committed for treatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not admitted to the ward after any criminal offence but because of his restlessness and agitation, both of which, restlessness and agitation, were treated during hospitalisation. So that at the moment he was discharged, he was no longer dangerous for the environment. Had there been such a danger, I would have certainly informed my mentor, and we would have, through legal proceedings, prevented his discharge, the discharge of a dangerous patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet asked you whether or not the mental disorder that he was suffering at the time could have been provoked by alcohol, and you used the term "alcohol-provoked psychosis," and you said that you would need other reports to make that determination. As the person who was the primary mental health caregiver to Mr. Vasiljevic, absent those reports, I ask you to rely on your recollection and ask you: Is it possible that the disorder that you observed was the result of his alcoholism?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the existence of case histories from earlier courses of treatment, it may be assumed that the disease alcoholism, given uninterrupted consumption under extraordinary conditions and a high level of stress when life is at risk, coupled with the loss of loved ones, can result in the development of a psychotic disorder. In this case, I was not able to comment in any great detail about this because I simply have not had access to documents about his earlier treatment because the patient came from another state where there was a state of emergency and his wife did not bring the necessary documents with her, so that at that point in time, we didn't have complete insight into his disease. And this is also noted in the discharge document that I myself wrote out. I said that the first -- that this was the first hospitalisation, though there is evidence of earlier treatment, though -- but I didn't see it. I didn't have access to the appropriate document. So that, having what I had, all I could suggest was unspecific psychosis, giving a picture of an acute and transient psychotic disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, during your treatment of Mr. Vasiljevic, it would have been helpful to have had these documents and records from his earlier treatments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would. The documents could assist possibly in determining the etiological factor with greater precision, that is, the cause of the development of the psychotic disorder, which means that his psychotic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. disorder could be categorised as so-called alcoholic psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Had you known then that he had been treated on a number of occasions for his alcoholism, would that have changed your diagnosis, this 289.9, I believe it was, this -- sorry, 298.9, this diagnosis you wrote in the case history? Might that have altered what you wrote as your concluding diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Ninth Classification of Disease, alcoholic psychoses of that kind were grouped under this code 298.9, unspecific psychoses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have a specific recollection today whether when you wrote or when you classified him as 298.9, whether it was your opinion that he had alcoholic psychosis or whether he had this unclassified psychosis unrelated to alcoholism? Do you have a clear memory of your determination today?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 298.9, this diagnosis is a diagnosis which combines into one all psychotic disorders which produce a similar clinical picture regardless of the etiology.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, under the Tenth Classification, the current classification, would it still be considered F23.0? I'm sorry, alcoholism -- alcoholic psychosis, would that also be classified as F23.0?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the new Tenth Classification, if one has all the documents and full insight into the treatment given to the patient, most probably he would have been diagnosed F10.3 -- .5. Sorry. These are alcoholic psychoses. F10.3 -- .5. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I took a few notes when you were describing the symptoms. I want to go through them with you and ask you have I missed any. The symptoms, I believe you said, were agitation, disquiet, and disturbance of thought process. Were there any other symptoms that you observed of Mr. Vasiljevic during your treatment of him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by what one could see and hear when the patient was being admitted at the time, the other functions could not be judged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you -- maybe you can clarify that answer. Are you saying that there were other symptoms that you were not able to judge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mental functions can be tested in detail only if the patient is capable of controlling his behaviour and if he is not restless in terms of psycho-motor functions. Later, upon discharge, we see that he was regular, that he was quiet, and that the only visible symptom was that of a certain degree of acceleration, which most frequently means that his speech was rather accelerated and his movements were fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, you used the word "controlling his behaviour," and could you distinguish for us the difference between somebody who is angry and is being intentionally disruptive as opposed to somebody who has the inability to control his behaviour? Can you distinguish what you would look for to make that determination?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone who is intentionally disruptive has to make a pause. He cannot continue to simulate abnormal behaviour continuously for a long time, whereas a sick man, a patient, he shows disruptive behaviour continuously and pronounced restlessness which can be remedied only by applying the adequate therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in the case of Mr. Vasiljevic, can you describe -- was this symptom that you're describing now, was it interrupted or not interrupted?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by everything, one can conclude that it was uninterrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that diagnosis indicated anywhere on the papers that you now have before -- before you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 298.9, on the case history. On the case history and also on the discharge document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, you've told us now that 298.9 could have been alcoholic psychosis. If it were that, would these behaviours continue uninterrupted as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, it seems that 298.9, at this period of time, could cover a range of different psychoses, and my question is: Does inability to control one's behaviour over an uninterrupted basis, would that also be a symptom that one would expect to see in alcoholic psychoses?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 298.9 was a so-called service diagnosis, which means it covered a wide range of psychotic disorders, and it was very frequently used in classifications. His alcoholic psychosis came under that category, but all psychoses have their beginning treatment with identical medication. Regardless of the etiology in this case, alcoholic psychosis is treated with the same medicines as other psychoses, and it has a duration similar to that of other psychoses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just before we adjourn, Mr. Domazet, what do you want to do with these documents that you have produced, or should I say the one in B/C/S which you produced and the English translation which the Prosecution has produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to tender them as Defence Exhibit D30, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, the B/C/S original will be Exhibit D30, and the English translation will be D30.1. We will adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, I'd like to go back to your diagnosis of 298.9. Would every different type of psychosis classified under this 298.9 necessarily have what you've described as uncontrolled -- inability to control behaviour for an uninterrupted period of time? Would every diagnosis fitting into that category have to share that particular symptom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The other symptoms you mentioned were agitation. Can you give us an idea more precisely what you mean by agitation? How did it manifest itself in the behaviours of Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agitation is increased uncontrolled behaviour. For example, agitation, as I say, means increased uncontrolled behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would that symptom be also consistent with somebody suffering from alcoholic psychoses?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A psychotic picture would be almost identical, we have already said that, with manifestations and symptoms. Only later can we look at the etiology or, rather, the causes. But the clinical picture of acute psychosis, of acute psychotic disorder, in the vast majority of cases is either very similar or identical, regardless of etiology.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this symptom of agitation, can you give us, during the period he was on the psychiatric ward, during what period of time did he suffer from that symptom, particular symptom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is certain is that it was visible upon admission. As to the rest, it wasn't very precisely recorded in the case history, but a customary period for the duration of this kind of clinical picture, along with adequate therapy, would not be longer than one or two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you say "therapy," is that drug therapy, some medicines?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you say -- you used the word "visible." Would the manifestation of this symptom be only visible to somebody like yourself with specialised training or would other doctors and nurses in the hospital also be able to recognise these symptoms? Would they be visible to other medical personnel as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those symptoms are visible to anybody because the picture and expression of it is truly drastic. It is exceptionally conspicuous behaviour with a great deal of agitation and restlessness, and everybody would be able to recognise it without having any medical training at all. But perhaps they wouldn't know that it was a psychotic disorder. Usually people would say, "He's mad," something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in your experience, the onset of this symptom, is it something that happens rapidly or is it something that happens gradually over a period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Psychotic disorder to that degree, in that intensity in which he was in quite certainly was at its peak then, and that is precisely why he was transferred to the psychiatric ward. However, it may happen with a certain number of disorders - and alcoholic disorders come under that category - that he had certain manifestations of conspicuous behaviour which would -- and this could come from the environment, the family. But here in the case history, judging by the statements of his spouse, he was conspicuous, restless, and agitated. He would stay at work longer than was necessary. He behaved in a way which differed from his usual conduct, from what his behaviour had been up until then, before he was admitted into hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, are you saying that, based upon his wife's observations that he stayed at work longer than necessary and that his behaviour had changed, that you were able to say that he was suffering from psychoses before he arrived at the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say he suffered from psychosis before he came to hospital. What I said was that, judging by what his wife said, his wife's statements, his behaviour had been different and conspicuous. He wasn't hospitalised during that period but only when he came to the ward, so that we can only speak about the clinical picture upon admission because we didn't see him before that. We weren't able to see and assess him before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I don't want there to be some problem later about this. Your question was whether he -- the accused had been suffering from psychoses before he arrived at the psychiatric ward. The doctor has answered, as I understand it, before he came to the hospital. It may or may not be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think the doctor's answer probably encompasses what you're asking, but I don't want there to be any problem later about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: By the way, can you just remind me, I can't find the document here, if he was admitted on the 14th of June, what date was it that he was transferred to the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe it was the 7th -- he arrived on the 7th and an entry was made on the 8th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry, the 7th of July, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it was about three weeks after he is said to have been admitted to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, let's go back to the symptoms that you've described. Am I correct in characterising them as readily apparent to both medical personnel and non-medical personnel? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, what is the hospital procedure in a case where a patient presents themselves and they have both a serious mental disorder as well as a serious physical disorder? What procedure is followed in Uzice hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of a patient who is psychotic and exceptionally agitated, he is hospitalised in the psychiatric ward. Now, if he has an accompanying somatic disorder, then the relevant specialist service is consulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So can we conclude from the case history of Mr. Vasiljevic that at the time that he was brought -- initially brought to Uzice hospital, there was no readily apparent symptoms of a psychological disorder?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can conclude that he was admitted to another ward because of another disorder but that the psychiatrist did not examine him when he was actually admitted. He was only examined by a specialist of that branch of medicine for which he had a referral letter with the referral diagnosis. So when a patient comes to us with a referral letter for a certain specialist's service, he is examined by that particular specialist, and on the basis of that, a conclusion is drawn. Not all the specialists get to examine him upon admission, only the specialist for which he has received the referral diagnosis and referral letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But wouldn't we be correct in concluding that, upon his initial admission to Uzice, the admitting doctor saw no need for a psychiatric referral, to have somebody from your department go down and make an assessment of his psychological condition? We can conclude that from the record, can't we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the records, we can conclude that a psychiatrist was not consulted upon admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can we also conclude that, had he visibly demonstrated the symptoms you've described at the time of his admission to Uzice hospital, that the probable course of treatment would have been to assign him to the psychiatric ward and then to see to it that orthopaedic specialists took care of whatever orthopaedic injuries needed tending to? Can we conclude that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can conclude that the patient was admitted at the orthopaedic ward, and judging by what could be seen, he had a grave injury. With a grave injury of that kind, even if he was psychotic, he could not have done -- he could not have expressed his psychotic condition much because he was probably under the effects of pain and immobilisation and the fear he had of the injury sustained. So that his agitation could have passed as being a reaction to the injury itself. And then injuries of that kind are emergency states, so that is why he was admitted immediately, operated on, and therefore, the psychiatrist was consulted only later, once he had begun to show manifest signs of psychotic behaviour in the course of his hospitalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, you're speculating now about what may or may not have been done regarding his treatment initially; correct? You do not know this by personal knowledge, do you, or by any record that you have?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody examined him. None of the psychiatrists examined him upon admission. I don't think I'm speculating. I am just -- I am basing my statement and opinion on the recorded entries in the case history where we see that it was a serious fracture where surgery was administered. He was operated on. So I was not speculating as to his physical somatic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But are you suggesting that, over the course of three weeks, that he may have received painkillers that could have suppressed or masked the psychotic symptoms which you've described for us? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Analgetics, certainly not. They would not. Not analgetics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And do you know of any medication or drug that he was receiving at that time which, in your opinion, would have masked or suppressed the symptoms of psychoses?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have an insight into his therapy list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, one of the things we've heard here in this case is that he was in traction. Now, given that, when he arrived at the psychiatric ward he needed to be tied up, would you not agree with me that if he was so agitated and so nervous and exhibiting these symptoms, that he would have been causing injury to his leg that was being immobilised through traction? Would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was immobilised, is that what you're asking? I'm not sure I followed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm -- it seems that you're unable to tell us precisely when, but soon after his arrival in the psychiatric ward, he was actually tied to his bed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that whatever behaviours that he was engaged in that required you direct the staff to tie him to his bed, that if he were exhibiting those same behaviours at the time when he was placed in traction, his leg was in traction with the weight, that those same behaviours would have jeopardised his recovery, the recovery of his broken leg? Would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a sort of an assumption as well. We cannot speak with any precision about that because nobody examined him. None of the psychiatrists examined him at that time. And in the realm of speculation, the staff of the orthopaedics ward might not have recognised psychotic behaviour as such so that it is -- they would not have been duty-bound to recognise a psychosis. But quite obviously, they did react when this took on larger proportions, when the -- when his behaviour was unhinged to a greater extent, and then they consulted psychiatrists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to the alcoholic psychosis that you've told us about, and the question I want to ask you: Is it not true that that particular psychosis is triggered when the person abstains from alcohol? When they cease their daily intake of alcohol, that's when we start to see the onset of that particular type of psychosis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the foundations of all types of psychotic disorders. So this is a global disturbance or impairment of the central nervous system. So a global impairment of the central nervous system which is manifest in the symptoms described where disturbed behaviour, loss of control of impulse, restlessness, agitation, and other symptoms come into play, depending on whether the psychosis was caused by alcohol. Alcohol is a factor which led to this global impairment of the central nervous system. If the patient is a dependent, is alcohol dependent, then he always has what we call the abstinence syndrome or withdrawal syndrome; that is to say, the appearance of the lust for alcohol and the need for the substance upon which he is dependent. It can happen that when the quantity of the substance is reduced that the manifestations of abstinence become visible. However, the most frequent cause of a psychosis is a global impairment to the brain and not the abstinence syndrome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, would I be correct in saying that one of the symptoms of -- brought on by alcohol abstinence, by a person who is a severe alcoholic, would be agitation? Wouldn't that be a symptom you would expect to see when the person no longer has alcohol? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, please, could you repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would the symptom of agitation not also be a symptom which we see when a person who is heavily dependent on alcohol no longer has alcohol, one of the withdrawal symptoms? Wouldn't agitation be one of those symptoms?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That isn't the rule. It is individual, depending on the person and depending on the state of the central nervous system in the first place, the length that alcohol has been consumed, the intensity, the general condition of the body, and many other factors both internal and external, so that you cannot set clear hard and fast rules, because each patient is a case in himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to set clear and hard, fast rules. What I'm asking you, is the symptom of agitation a possible symptom of withdrawal syndrome, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. The abstinence syndrome or withdrawal syndrome, manifestation of that can sometimes be a certain degree of restlessness, tenseness, but the abstinence syndrome does not absolutely imply psychotic -- a psychotic condition. It is a separate entity. The abstinence syndrome has its own level, and it is a level of restlessness, tension, nervousness, and need for the substance. But a psychotic disorder is drastically -- on a drastically higher level and much stronger, and when that appears, it is classified in quite a different way. So this was not an abstinence syndrome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you saying that your observations of Mr. Vasiljevic, that it is your opinion that he was not suffering from alcohol abstinence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was suffering from it, if he did have the symptoms of abstinence, they were not recorded, because upon arrival at the ward, about three weeks went by and the abstinence -- he should have felt the abstinence syndrome as soon as he stopped taking the substance, not three weeks later, not after spending three weeks in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, let me ask you for the purposes of my question to assume something different, not that he had been in the hospital three weeks, but let's say he had been in the hospital a matter of days and he'd only ceased to have alcohol for a matter of days before you saw him. Would the symptoms that you saw in him be consistent with the symptoms one would expect to find of somebody in the process of withdrawal from alcohol?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a psychotic disturbance and not an abstinence syndrome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you can say to us with certainty that none of the symptoms that you observed in Mr. Vasiljevic had anything whatsoever to do with withdrawal from alcohol?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody can say that, but what in a psychotic disorder is manifest Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is a drastic, drastic level of disorder and disturbance so that there is nobody who would be able to differentiate and say whether a psychotic patient also has elements of abstinence, because the psychosis is an enormous global disorder. What we have here is a patient who, after three weeks, was brought to the psychiatric ward, so that means that abstinence syndromes must have appeared and become manifest earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us, once somebody ceases to have alcohol, how much time passes before we can see the onset of withdrawal symptoms?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, he would have to have been suffering from dependence, a sick -- dependence sickness for an abstinence syndrome to set in, and it is a diagnostic criteria for a dependency disease or addiction. Some patients who take in alcohol do not develop the addiction or dependence disease. Where the dependency disease is involved, abstinence comes into play very soon afterwards, that means between 24 and 48 hours after they have ceased to take the substance. In drastic cases, it would set in, that is to say, the pre-delirium syndrome would set in, which means a trembling and shaking of the hands, increased perspiration, fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you see any of these symptoms manifest themselves in Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those symptoms were not seen in Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to show you a document, and I ask that it be marked as Prosecution document number 165. I'll ask that the doctor be shown the original and the copies are for the Court. There is an English translation at the end of this document. I apologise that it is not marked, but I would ask that that be deemed Prosecution document 165.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. Is 165 three pages long and then this document attached to the back, that's intended to be 165.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, make sure the doctor's got the English translation, because he seems to have all the yellow sheets. Oh, he probably doesn't need the translation so it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it's his document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise Prosecution document 165?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the therapy list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does this sheet or list indicate all of the medications that Mr. Vasiljevic received while he was in the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that the earliest page is the last page, that we're in reverse order? This document is in reverse order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has just been attached in that way, joined. Otherwise, the order goes from the last page towards the front page. Otherwise, that's it. The order has just been changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to go to the third page, to the date of the 8th of July, and ask you is that the first time that medications were administered to Mr. Vasiljevic on the psychiatric ward?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as a patient is admitted, this therapy list is prepared and all the medicines administered necessarily have to be entered. And we see here that the list was opened on the 7th, on the 7th of July, and that the patient received vials, injections, in this case Topral, which is a very strong anti-psychotic, every eight hours, which supports his condition of pronounced restlessness, because this is therapy for very grave restlessness. And we see that he received these injections for another six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, before I ask you specific questions about this, is this the therapy sheet that was used in the treatment of Mr. Vasiljevic and which you and other staff recorded the treatments on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you see any strange markings or markings that you do not believe were on the original document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the original document, and this Largactil is in my handwriting, and I added on these -- the medicines. Largactil was written out by me, and the Novalgetol vials, probably because of pain on the 21st, was also written by me. And this other handwriting -- do I need to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll ask you a few questions in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender Prosecution document 165 and 165.1 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be exhibits P165 and 165.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now Doctor, let's go back to Topnal [phoen] first. Is Topnal [phoen] a sedative?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an anti-psychotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe for us what effects it has on the patient?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of the strongest anti-psychotics, and it affects -- its effect is to calm psycho-motor disturbance and agitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it used to treat any other type of illness or psychological problem other than outright psychoses?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the next drug on this list, can you please tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is called Nozinan. Generically, it is Levomepromazin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, for the benefit, to make sure that the record is accurate, could I ask you to first spell Topnal, the correct spelling of Topnal.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: T-O-P-R-A-L.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to spell this next drug, Nozinan.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: N-O-Z-I-N-A-N.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you spell its generic equivalent?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. Could the witness repeat the word, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: L-E-V-O-M-E-P-R-O-M-A-Z-E-N. L at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, do you read English?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you, is it correctly spelled on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First is L.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And other than that, it's correctly spelled?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, can you --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. After Z, E-N.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you could start again, Doctor. But before you do, I'm glad to say that it was not me in the transcript who tried to pronounce it earlier. Could you just spell it from the beginning, slowly, Doctor, so we can get the whole thing down.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: L-E-V-O-M-E-P-R-O-M-A-Z-I-N.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have a look at it in the transcript, if you would, at line 11. Is it correctly spelt there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Congratulations to the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, Topral, could you tell us what the generic equivalent of Topral is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you. It is a drug that we obtained through humanitarian aid so that now I'm unable to give any details about it. We used it at the time. It is no longer used in clinical practice. For the last ten years, I haven't come across this drug.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the last drug that's indicated on this therapy sheet, can you please tell us the name as it appears here and spell it for us.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: H-L-O-R-P-R-O-M-A-Z-I-N.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
