utterances.text: So in your opinion, that was the day he was transferred, that would be the 7th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I was mentioning a few incidents that preceded his hospitalisation, as testified by the accused and others, that occurred some 15 days prior to his admission, but from the moment he was admitted until he arrived at your ward, if it is proven that, while hospitalised, your patient sang, insulted other patients and behaved in a way that stood out from the behaviour of other patients, would that also be a preliminary symptom of the disorder that developed later, on the 7th of July at the latest?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is conspicuous behaviour, and it can be an indication of the gradual development of a psychosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the fact, Dr. Simic, that this disorder or disease has been identified by you as a serious mental illness, could it have set in suddenly, on one particular day, be it the 7th of July or some other day, or do the preceding events gradually lead to the outbreak of the disease?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The psychotic level of his behaviour or drastic disturbance was experienced the moment he was admitted, but the conspicuous behaviour certainly fits within his basic behavioural disorder; singing, shouting, aggressiveness. And on the 7th of July, this reached a climax.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Simic, when you were answering questions before you were shown exhibit -- that is, the therapy sheet that you reviewed and commented on later on, before you saw any written document, on the basis merely of your recollection, you said that in such cases, with adequate treatment, a patient, in one or two days, recovers to a point and is no longer in a condition that he has to be tied up. When you saw the documents and everything that was done with respect to this specific patient, Mitar Vasiljevic, do you still abide by what you said or was his case more serious than you thought, requiring a stronger therapy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the therapy sheet, he was for six days extremely restless, which is a little longer than is usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So what you said before, was that the average or customary in the case of such patients and later on your comments were based on the actual documents you had before you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Doctor, I have several questions concerning Exhibit 138. Please look at Exhibit 138, page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got it there, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I don't have it. I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be produced for you in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Please look at page 1. You said you typed the figures in column 12. That is to say, "Psychosis," and "298.9." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Does that mean that those figures in columns other than 12 were typed into by other doctors or nurses?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I typed in "Psychosis" in column 12, also the date, that is column 13, and I am the second signatory under column 17, the doctor who treated the patient. My name is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Then please look at column 3. Usually who, what kind of doctor or nurse, is entitled to type into column 3?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this is typed in by the admissions service, the nurse in the admissions or the reception, and the diagnoses are typed in by the doctors. The discharge is also typed by doctors. The date and type of operation is also typed by doctors, and the signatures are also typed by doctors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: By looking through Exhibit 138, can you tell who typed column 3 in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. Probably the nurse who was on duty at the admissions department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: The figures in columns other than 12 seem to be typed by the same kind of typing machine of yours. The same type of typing machines as yours were used by other doctors and nurses in Uzice hospital Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that, but I think that the typewriting differs, if we look closely. I don't think it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Even now, you use the same typing machine?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The typewriters are 20 to 30 years old, so that probably they're still using them. But I'm in a different hospital now. But my typewriter, this typewriter, is probably still in that hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do counsel want to ask questions arising out of that? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for coming along to give evidence and for the evidence which you gave. I'm sorry you've had such a long time but it's been a very important issue that you've been discussing and we are very grateful to you for your assistance. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the next witness, might I inform that Court we are in possession of the ledgers now. Unfortunately, because of some personal problems, I've not been able to look at them last night or at lunchtime today. I will endeavour to look at them tonight and tomorrow morning. I would advise the Court that we have attempted to contact the forensic examiner for the last three days and have been unable to. As soon as we contact him, we will try to get an estimate of how long it will take and give that to the Court. And I believe now the only documents I would -- I don't believe that I'll be seeking to examine any additional documents than were put in the original order, although I would like to reserve final determination on that until I've had an opportunity just to look at those other books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I gather that the next witness is a nurse in the orthopaedic department. I don't know whether we're going to take her through all of those documents. I hope we're not. But if we are, they better stay in the courtroom, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have the psychiatric one, and I will have somebody sent up to bring down the other ones now so they're available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, madam, will you please make the solemn declaration in the document which the court usher has handed you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam.

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will be asking you questions on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Vasiljevic, so will you please, when you hear my question, pause a little before giving your answer because of the interpretation and since we both speak the same language. Let me first ask you to introduce yourself to the Court and give us your basic particulars; your name, date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: My name is Slavica Pavlovic. I was born in Uzice on the 18th of August, 1957.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mrs. Pavlovic, what is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: I have eight years elementary schooling and secondary medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where are you employed now?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: I'm employed at the general hospital in Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since when have you been working in the general hospital in Uzice, Mrs. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: I have been working since the 1st of December, 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that you have been fully employed without interruption since 1986 at the Uzice general hospital?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, in which ward at the hospital were you working?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: I was working in the ward for orthopaedic surgery and traumatology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After that, are you still working in the same ward or department?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please describe your ward in 1992, as far as you can remember; which were the doctors working there, how many rooms you had, and which part of the hospital you occupied.

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: In 1992, our ward was on the fourth floor of the hospital, and it is still there. We had 18 rooms. They were numbers from 401 to 418. They still bear the same numbers but two of those rooms are not patients' rooms. Then we had doctors, Dr. Milosavljevic, who was head of the department at the time; Dr. Jovicevic who, in those days, was also the director of the hospital; Dr. Vojkan Krnjic; and also Dr. Djordje Stojkovic. Those were the orthopaedics. And in addition to them, there were doctors who were preparing for specialisation courses or were already specialising in orthopaedics; Dr. Ivan Jovanovic and Dr. Vladimir Gordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have you remembered the names of all the doctors or have you omitted anyone?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: I am sure I told you the names of all the orthopaedists who were there. May I do it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No. Let me ask you specifically about one. Was he working in your department or some other department?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: I am sorry. I omitted to mention Dr. Moljevic. Yes, I forgot him for a moment. He was working in our department at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. So he was working in your department as well?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, what were your duties as nurses regarding keeping records of patients?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: Patients came to our department with their case history already issued, and these case histories are opened at the admissions department of our hospital. Once they arrive to our department, it is our duty to register them in our notebook if they arrive prior to 1300 hours. We also open temperature charts. And if they arrive after 1.00 p.m., then the shift registers them in the handover/takeover notebook, handover/takeover of duty notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Before you continue, will you please explain what kind of shifts you had, how many shifts there were, and were there records of those shifts?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: Of course there were records. The nurses worked in shifts and there were three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell us how they went.

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: The first started at 6.00 a.m. and went on until 1.00 p.m. The second shift started at 1.00 p.m. and ended at 2000 hours, at 8.00 p.m. And the third shift started at 8.00 p.m. and ended at 6.00 a.m. That was the work in shifts of the secondary medical staff, medical staff with secondary education.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did this first shift coincide with the regular working hours of doctors and nurses in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: This was work in shifts, but the people who only worked the first shift, they worked until 2.00 p.m., doctors from 7.00 a.m. until 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So the regular working hours of both doctors and nurses, excluding the shifts, were from 7.00 a.m. until 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: Yes, for the doctors; but for the nurses, from 6.00 a.m. until Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was there a separate record book of the handover of shifts? Was there a special notebook for that?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: Yes, there was a notebook. This notebook would be filled in by the second and third shifts. There was a special notebook which we referred to as the handover/takeover notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us why such records were not kept during the first shift?

utterances.speaker: Slavica Pavlovic.
utterances.text: In the first shift, we had another notebook for results where we entered the patients who were received, admitted in the course of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this might be a convenient time for us to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume again at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of November, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.00 p.m.,
